newsitem.title: RUSSIA: N.Korea launches new calendar to honour Kim -Tass.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea launches new calendar to honour Kim -Tass.

text.p: Stalinist North Korea has changed its calendar to honour its late "Great Leader" Kim Il-sung and his ideology of "juche" (self-reliance), Itar-Tass news agency said on Wednesday.

In a story filed from the reclusive state's capital Pyongyang, Tass said that 1912, the year of Kim's birth, would mark the start of the new calendar "when the Great Leader rose high like the sun of juche".
It said April 15, Kim's birthday, would now be known as the Festival of the Sun.
The decisions were part of a resolution approved by the all-powerful Workers' Party on Tuesday, the third anniversary of Kim's death which also marked the end of official mourning, Tass said.

"By beating a path hitherto untrodden, the Great Leader Comrade Kim Il-sung led the struggle of our people for socialist revolution and the construction of socialism along the direct road to victory," the resolution said.
Earlier on Wednesday Tass quoted North Korea's envoy in Moscow as saying he was sure the country's effective ruler Kim Jong-il, the Great Leader's son, would formally assume top state positions soon.

"Kim Jong-il, undoubtedly, is our leader without any elections or appointments," Tass quoted ambassador Son Song Pil as saying. "I think he will be elevated to the top positions, but there have been no decisions on when and in what form."
The ambassador, who is a senior figure in the North Korean hierarchy, has previously hinted Kim Jong-il could be appointed supreme leader of the party and state as soon as the mourning ended.
Since his father's death, Kim Jong-il, now 55, has established full personal control but the formal top party post and the state presidency have been left vacant.

Western political analysts have said there are no indications North Korea is preparing a succession ceremony for Kim Jong-il and have suggested the actual dynastic succession is not likely to occur in the next few months.
North Korea was a long-time ally of the now-defunct Soviet Union but ties with Russia are less solid because Moscow has turned increasingly to other countries, including South Korea.
International aid officials say many North Koreans are near starvation and could die in the next few months unless food arrives.
Food is being shipped to North Korea by Christian organisations and volunteers. Tass said Russia was also planning to send humanitarian food aid.
